objectives.text: Name the four broad functions of water in the body.
Explain how electrolytes govern the movement of water between compartments.
Describe how water balance is regulated and what triggers thirst.
State the consequences of dehydration, including its link to heat stroke.
Explain what a free radical is and how it damages a cell.
Say why antioxidant-rich foods are supported by evidence where supplements are not.

terms.gloss: A dissolved mineral carrying a charge — sodium, potassium, chloride. Their concentration decides where water goes.
Water's nickname: more substances dissolve in it than in any other fluid.
Water output exceeding intake. It lowers blood volume and is a primary cause of heat stroke.
An unstable molecule with an unpaired electron, produced unavoidably by normal metabolism.
A substance that donates an electron to a free radical, interrupting the damage it would otherwise do.
A plant compound that is not a nutrient but appears to contribute to reduced disease risk.

questions.prompt: Water moves between body compartments mainly in response to:
options: The concentration of dissolved electrolytes
The total volume of fluid that a person drinks
How much protein is present in the diet
The temperature of the surrounding air
questions.why: The body does not push water around directly. It moves electrolytes, and water follows the concentration gradient.
distractorNotes: Intake matters, but it is not the mechanism of distribution.
Plasma proteins play a part, but electrolytes govern it.
Temperature affects loss, not distribution.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of water's four broad functions?
options: Supplying energy to working cells
Acting as a transportation vehicle
Serving as the universal solvent
Helping to regulate temperature
questions.why: Water is a macronutrient because it is needed in quantity, but it yields no energy at all.
distractorNotes: One of the four — it carries nutrients and waste.
One of the four — more dissolves in it than anything else.
One of the four — sweat and blood flow move heat.

options: A coordinated hormonal and neural response
A simple reflex triggered by a dry mouth
A conscious decision made about fluid intake
A signal that appears only after dehydration
questions.why: Several hormones and neural signals combine to defend fluid balance. A dry mouth is a symptom along the way, not the trigger.
distractorNotes: Dry mouth accompanies thirst; it does not cause it.
The drive is involuntary, whatever you then choose.
It generally begins before dehydration is established.

questions.prompt: Dehydration is a primary cause of heat stroke because it:
options: Lowers blood volume and limits cooling
Raises the body's core temperature directly
Reduces the amount of salt in the blood
Prevents the skin from absorbing water
questions.why: Less blood volume means less capacity to carry heat to the skin and to sweat, so the body loses its main way of shedding heat.
distractorNotes: It undermines cooling; it is not itself a heat source.
Sodium concentration typically rises.
Skin does not absorb water for this purpose.

questions.prompt: A free radical is damaging because it:
options: Steals electrons from nearby molecules
Blocks enzymes from reaching a substrate
Occupies space that a nutrient would use
Lowers the acidity inside the cell body
questions.why: It takes electrons from lipids, proteins, RNA and DNA, damaging each in turn and often creating another radical.
distractorNotes: Not the mechanism described.
Not a space problem.
Not how the damage works.

questions.prompt: Free radicals in the body are:
options: An unavoidable by-product of metabolism
Produced only by pollution and by smoking
Created solely during heavy exercise
Present only in people who are unwell
questions.why: Normal cellular metabolism generates them continuously. External sources add to a load that already exists.
distractorNotes: Those add to the load but are not the only source.
Exercise adds to it; it is not the sole source.
Everyone produces them all the time.

questions.prompt: What does the evidence support about antioxidants?
options: Antioxidant-rich foods reduce disease risk
High-dose supplements reliably reduce risk
Supplements work better than whole foods
Antioxidants have no measurable effect
questions.why: Foods rich in antioxidants are supported. High-dose supplements are not, and some evidence suggests they can do harm.
distractorNotes: Supplement claims are not backed, and may carry risk.
The evidence runs the other way.
Overcorrection — the food evidence is real.

questions.prompt: Why might an antioxidant help at low dose but not at high?
options: Benefit does not scale without limit
Absorption stops above a fixed amount
High doses are destroyed by stomach acid
The body excretes everything above the RDA
questions.why: More is not simply better. Antioxidants and phytochemicals appear beneficial in the amounts food supplies, not in concentrated doses.
distractorNotes: Absorption is not the explanation given.
Not the mechanism.
Not true of all of them.

questions.prompt: Beverages differ from solid food in that they:
options: Satisfy thirst without satisfying hunger
Are absorbed before reaching the stomach
Contain no calories worth counting daily
Are digested by a separate set of enzymes
questions.why: Drinks quench thirst rather than filling you, which is why calories drunk are easy to miss. They average about a fifth of daily intake.
distractorNotes: Absorption still happens downstream.
They supply about 21 percent of daily calories.
No separate enzyme system exists.

questions.prompt: Sodium and potassium sit at different concentrations across a cell membrane because:
options: That difference is what lets water be moved
Sodium cannot cross a cell membrane at all
Potassium is too large to leave a cell body
The two minerals never mix inside the body
questions.why: Maintaining different solute concentrations on either side gives the body a way to direct water between compartments.
distractorNotes: Sodium crosses, under control.
Potassium moves too.
They coexist throughout the body.

checklist: Estimate your fluid intake across one day, drinks and food.
Name two electrolytes and say what each does for fluid balance.
Describe one situation that would raise your needs and say why.
Name one antioxidant-rich food and cite where its evidence comes from.
selfCheck: Did I distinguish antioxidant foods from antioxidant supplements?
Did I explain water movement through electrolytes rather than by itself?
applicationPrompts.aiPolicy: These are questions for you to answer. This app does not write any part of a submission.
